info.bio:
Michael "Mike" Nesmith fué uno de los integrantes del grupo The Monkees (único músico real de la banda).
Nacido en Texas, luego de terminar el "proyecto" The Monkees, formó el grupo: Michael Nesmith And The First National Band con el que grabó solo dos Lps. consiguiendo un solo éxito: "Silver Moon".
Actualmente sigue su carrera solista y se presenta en vivo esporadicamente.

scenes.name: The Monkees
scenes.author: Jon Savage
scenes.desc: El pop aborrece el vacío: justo cuando los Beatles desaparecían, la industria promocionó su simulacro, cuatro chicos guapos reunidos tras mucha investigación para protagonizar una serie de televisión a lo A Hard Day’s Night. «Last Train to Clarksville», un acróstico contagioso de «Paperback Writer» con el tema oportuno de las despedidas forzosas de Vietnam, llegó al número 1. Si los Beatles no estaban, la industria los clonaría, y a los adolescentes más jóvenes les daba igual.

scenes.name: Segunda invasión británica y MTV
scenes.book: Postpunk. Romper todo y empezar de nuevo
scenes.author: Simon Reynolds
scenes.desc: En 1982 el new pop deja de ser un sueño de periodistas: «Don't You Want Me», «Tainted Love» y «The Look of Love» anuncian una nueva invasión, y en 1983 la segunda camada (Duran Duran, Culture Club, Wham!, Eurythmics, Thompson Twins) conquista Estados Unidos gracias a MTV, canal ideado por Michael Nesmith que, sin vídeos americanos, dependía de los británicos, más videogénicos y cultivados en el estilo («I want my MTV»). A Flock of Seagulls, Altered Images («Happy Birthday»), Simple Minds («Promised You a Miracle», New Gold Dream), Haircut 100, Kajagoogoo; Bowie se broncea con «Let's Dance». El new pop reexporta música negra (Chic, P-Funk, Quincy Jones) a la América blanca. En el Reino Unido, 1983 se vive en cambio como un año infausto: reelección de Thatcher, «Kill Ugly Pop» en las paredes y la vuelta de la conciencia social.

mentions.text: Nickelodeon, propiedad de Warner Brothers, empresa a la cual Nesmith también le propuso crear un canal dedicado exclusivamente a emitir videos promocionales de música las veinticuatro horas. Sin embargo, el canal pronto se alejó de las nociones más artísticas de Nesmith, quien renunció poco después para grabar su propio "álbum en video", Elephant Parts. podcast.title: Source of "The Tragically Hip" Name (1981)
podcast.body: The name "The Tragically Hip" was taken from a line in a 1981 video collection of music and comedy produced by Mike Nesmith, a former member of The Monkees. The specific line was part of a skit about fundraising for "poor yuppies" to sustain their lifestyles of Lamborghinis and cocaine. "That was stolen from a line in a 1981 video collection of music and comedy by Mike Nessmith, ex of the monkeys. The skit had to do with raising money for poor yuppies to keep them in Lamborghini's and cocaine. They were the so-called tragically hip."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Connection to The Tragically Hip Name
podcast.body: Michael Nesmith, a video pioneer and former member of The Monkees, produced the 1981 VHS tape "Elephant Parts," which contained a skit from which The Tragically Hip took their name. "This was produced by video pioneer and former member of the monkeys Michael Nessmith."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Dislike for Music Categorization
podcast.body: Michael Nesmith believed that attempting to categorize music, including the "country rock" label, was a "waste of time." He expressed a general aversion to such classifications. "Nessmith said though that he thinks it's a waste of time to try to categorize music at all and he also did not like the country rock label."

podcast.title: Founding The First National Band
podcast.body: After achieving fame with The Monkees in the 1960s, Michael Nesmith was a member of The First National Band, which is recognized as one of the earliest country rock groups. Despite this, he personally did not appreciate the "country rock" label. "Michael Nessmith, who became very famous as a member of the monkeys in the 1960s, was part of one of the first country rock bands after that."

podcast.title: Origin of "The Tragically Hip" Name
podcast.body: The phrase "the tragically hip," which the band adopted as their name, was a throwaway line found in a VHS tape full of skits released by Mike Nesmith, formerly of The Monkees. "The tragically hip, which was a throwaway phrase in a VHS tape full of skits, released by Mike Nessmith, formerly of the monkeys."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Real Musician in Fictional Band
podcast.body: Michael Nesmith was a real person, an actor and musician, who was hired to play a fictional musician within The Monkees, a band created for a television show. "But Michael Naysmith... these were real people. They were actors and musicians hired to pay fictional musicians seemingly inspired by the Beatles."

xref.title: Formation and Name Origin (1984)
xref.body: The Tragically Hip formed in 1984 in Kingston, Ontario, with Gord Downie (20 years old at the time), Gord Sinclair, Robbie Baker, Johnny Faye, and sax player Dave Manning (about 15 years older). They took their name from a skit in a 1981 VHS tape called "Elephant Parts," produced by video pioneer Michael Nesmith (formerly of The Monkees). The phrase "tragically hip" also appears in Elvis Costello's 1982 song "Town Cryer" from the "Imperial Bedroom" album. "Things started coming together in 1984 when Gord, then 20 years old, the other Gord, Robbie, Johnny Faye, and a sax player, about 15 years older than everyone named Dave Manning, formed the tragically hip, taking their name from a skit in a 1981 VHS tape making the rounds called Elephant Parts."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Connection to The Tragically Hip Name
xref.body: The phrase "tragically hip" appears in Elvis Costello's 1982 song "Town Cryer," which is featured on his "Imperial Bedroom" album. This was noted as a detail for "sticklers," alongside the band's primary inspiration from a Michael Nesmith skit. "that same phrase, tragically hip, shows up in an Elvis Costello song entitled Town Cryer in 1982."
